title: Sleep as trust
hookLine: I will lay me down in peace and sleep (Psalm 4:8)
tomorrow: what does a day look like with all of this in it?

cards: Two in the morning, eyes on the ceiling, the brain running tomorrow's list. Sleep won't take orders. Mark has a scene that's the opposite.

A boat in a storm, waves breaking in until it's filling with water, the disciples terrified. And in the back of the boat, Jesus is asleep on a pillow. They shake him awake: “Master, carest thou not that we perish?”

teach.h: SOMEONE ELSE HAS THE NIGHT WATCH.
teach.b: So how can anyone sleep with so much unfinished? The Psalms answer with trust. Psalm four: “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.”
Psalm one hundred twenty-one gives the reason: “he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.” Someone else has the night watch. Lying down becomes a small act of trust.
That's the sleep in the boat; when Jesus wakes, he says to the sea, “Peace, be still.” The Psalms are honest the other way too: “Thou holdest mine eyes waking.” This isn't a promise of a good night.
It's a way to lie down. Now a neighbor. Muslims have bedtime words too.

teach.h: IN YOUR NAME I DIE AND I LIVE.
teach.b: The hadith collection of al-Bukhari reports that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, would say on lying down, in effect: in your name, O God, I die and I live; and on waking, praise to God who gave us life after causing us to die.
Both traditions treat sleep as a handing over, and waking as a gift.

The honest difference: Muslims say those words following the Prophet's own practice, in their faith; Christian night prayer borrows Jesus' words from the cross in Luke: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.”
Different words, different faiths, and in both, the night handed to God.

how: Some Christians say a line from Psalm 4 or Psalm 3 as they lie down, and some end the day by handing over their worries in prayer before sleep.

treating dreams as messages from God
lying down as a way of handing the night to God

games.q: a parent's six-year-old asks why Grandma prays before bed. what's one sentence the parent could say at dinner?
o: she's asking God to promise nothing bad will ever happen.
she's making up for what she did wrong during the day.
she hands the night to God, so she can rest while God keeps watch.
games.why: Psalm 4 and Psalm 121: lie down in peace, because the keeper neither slumbers nor sleeps. Muslims, too, hand over the night in the Prophet's bedtime words.

practice: Sit back and let your hands fall open in your lap, palms up. On each out-breath, set down one thing you were planning to keep watch over tonight.
If you pray, borrow Psalm four as you go: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep.

wordCard.voice: Sleep as trust. Lying down as a way of handing the night to God, because someone else keeps watch.

orig.note: Mark's Greek for the pillow Jesus slept on in the storm.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: in peace, sleep, because the night watch isn't yours to keep. Rest well.
